title: Salim Kumar, National Award-Winning Malayalam Actor, Dies at 56 After Cardiac Arrest
excerpt: The beloved comedian and dramatic actor, best known for films like Meesa Madhavan and his award-winning role in Adaminte Makan Abu, passed away in Kochi following a long battle with multiple health complications.
body:
Malayalam cinema lost one of its most versatile performers on the night of 6 June when Salim Kumar, the actor who could make millions laugh and then break their hearts in the same breath, died of cardiac arrest at a private hospital in Kochi. He was 56.

A Career That Defied Categories

Born on 10 October 1969 in Chittatukara, North Paravur, Ernakulam district, Kumar began as a mimicry artist on stage before transitioning to television comedy and eventually to film with Ishtamanu Nooru Vattam in 1997.

Through the 2000s, he became the defining comic presence in Malayalam cinema's most commercially successful period. Films such as Meesa Madhavan, CID Moosa, Pulival Kalyanam, Chathikkatha Chanthu, Mayavi, and Kalyanaraman turned him into a household name across Kerala and among Malayali communities worldwide. His dialogue deliveries became cultural touchstones, and his scenes remain among the most shared content in Malayali internet culture.

But Kumar was far more than a comedian. In 2005, he won the Kerala State Film Award for Second Best Actor for Achanurangatha Veedu. Then came Adaminte Makan Abu in 2010 — a quiet, deeply humane film about an elderly Muslim couple saving for their Hajj pilgrimage. Kumar's performance earned him the National Film Award for Best Actor, a recognition that confirmed what audiences already sensed: that behind the comic timing lay genuine dramatic depth.

"Actor Salim Kumar had a face and expressions that Malayalis can never forget. I have lost someone who was like a brother to me."

— V.D. Satheesan, Chief Minister of Kerala

Health Struggles

Kumar's final years were marked by a punishing sequence of health crises. He was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis — a condition he publicly clarified was hereditary, not caused by alcohol — and underwent a liver transplant. He later developed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), chronic kidney disease requiring regular haemodialysis, and coronary artery disease.

In his final hospitalisation, Kumar was admitted with fever and breathing difficulties and placed on ventilator support. He received antibiotics, dialysis, and intensive treatment, but suffered a cardiac arrest from which he could not be revived, according to the hospital's medical bulletin. His death was confirmed at 10:43 PM on 6 June, reported The Hindu BusinessLine.

Tributes From India's Highest Offices

The outpouring of grief was immediate and crossed political and industry lines. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he was "deeply saddened" by the actor's passing, noting that Kumar "made a mark with his versatility and memorable performances across a wide range of roles."

Kerala Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, visibly emotional at a press conference, described Kumar as "deeply connected" and "fearless in his political beliefs." Satheesan noted that Kumar was a Congress supporter who had actively campaigned for the UDF in recent elections.

Industry peers including Mammootty, Prithviraj Sukumaran, and others from the Malayalam film fraternity paid tributes. MP Shashi Tharoor said he had met Kumar "a couple of times and found him just as delightful as in his many film roles."

Kumar was cremated with full state honours at his residence in North Paravur on 7 June. The Kerala government bore funeral expenses and arranged police honours including a bugle salute, according to Cinema Express.

A Legacy in 300 Films

Kumar's filmography spans more than 300 titles across three decades. Beyond his National Award, he collected four Kerala State Film Awards and a Filmfare Award South. His directorial venture Karutha Joothan won the 2017 Kerala State Film Award for Best Story.

For the millions of Malayalis living abroad — across the Gulf, North America, Europe, and Australia — Kumar was more than an entertainer. His characters captured something essential about Kerala's humour, warmth, and resilience, making him a cultural bridge between homeland and diaspora.
